title: Traxler Counterattack
description: One of the BEST openings for Black against White's very famous Fried Liver Attack. You will win many games in under 15 moves with massive attacks on your opponent's king.

r1b1k2N/pppp2pp/2n2n2/4p3/2B4q/4KQ2/PPPP.text: So, let's say the knight takes our rook.

r1b1k2N/pppp2pp/2n5/4p3/2B1n2q/4K3/PPPP2.text:
The knight takes on h8. 

This leads to a beautiful finish.

We have a forced checkmate, starting with Qf4+.

r1b1k2N/pppp2pp/2n5/4p3/2B1nq2/3K4/PPPP2.text:
The king goes to d3.

We'll play Nb4+ and force the king backwards. Mate is near.

r1b1k2N/pppp2pp/2n5/4p3/2B4q/6n1/PPPP3P/.text:
A lower percentage of games go like this. 

But we don't care about material in the Traxler: we care about attacking the white king! 

Our queen's knight leaps into the center.

r1b1k2N/pppp2pp/5n2/4p3/2Bn3q/4KQ2/PPPP2.text:
We can attack the queen. 

The attack on the queen is one thing, but the point is there are so many pieces around White's king. 

10.Qg3 Nf5+ is a nasty fork.

r1b1k2N/pppp2pp/8/4p3/1nB1n3/8/PPPPKqPP/.text:
Checkmate. 

Many finishes like this are possible if White messes up!

r1b1k2N/pppp2pp/8/4p3/2Bn1q2/8/PPPP4/RNB.text: The best thing we have here is a draw by repetition, if White can find all the correct moves, of course!

r1b1k2N/pppp2pp/8/4p3/2Bn3q/6P1/PPPP4/RN.text:
White is advised to capture on g3 now.

We'll recapture with check.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n2q/4K1P1/PP.text:
This move is the best, but White has to find it.

We can take on g3. 

Very important: with the idea of ...Qd4+ because ...Qxc4 isn't our goal. We want to attack the king. Material is out of the question for now.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n2q/4KQ2/PPP.text:
This move doesn't work.

Retreating our attacked knight wins the game. 

Our plan is ...Nd4 to continue the checkmate attack.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n2q/6P1/PPPP.text:
A simple way of defending is 8.g3, which has been seen in close to 50,000 games.

White can defend the f2-square with the queen, of course. But 8.Qf3 or Qf1 is met with 8...Rf8 and suddenly the knight on f7 is pinned! ...d5 and ...Nd4 would also cause problems.

We'll take on g3! Retreating is not an option! We have a draw at the very least, and a checkmate at best!

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B4q/4K1P1/PPPP.text:
White recaptures.

And we give a check to force the king to a bad file.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B4q/6P1/PPPP4/.text:
The pawn recaptures. 

This move is the most popular.

We'll take on g3 and give check.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B4q/6n1/PPPP3P.text:
We have a winning attack. We're threatening a discovered check on the king.

White can't even take our knight as the rook would fall with check and then more material will go afterwards.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B5/6q1/PPPP4/R.text: The king is forced to f1.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2Bq4/5KP1/PPPP4.text: On the f-file, we can do things with tempo.

r1b1kr2/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B5/6q1/PPPP4/R.text:
And we can pin the knight on f7. 

We have ideas of d5 to distract the bishop on c4 but also to play Bh3+.

White has to pray for a draw.

r1b2rk1/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2Bq4/5KP1/PPPP4.text: White's pieces are hanging. Believe it or not, the only move that doesn't lose here is 11.Rh4! We would then continue with e4+ and a wild position ensues which the engine evaluates as approximately equal. Your opponents are not engines though!

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/8/PPP.text:
About 63% of games go like this. 

White cannot resist forking us. But this is actually a mistake.

We take their f-pawn with check! This is The Traxler! 

The point is not material, but the fact that we'll be immediately attacking the king.

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.text:
Close to 60% of games feature 6.Kxf2, which is why we're seeing this first in our course. 

Since the king is vulnerable, we'll continue giving checks with aggression.

Our knight jumps in, capturing the e-pawn!

The white king won't know what to do. A good rule to remember is that the king loses by going to any light square!

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n3/4K3/PPPP2.text:
The other move that does not lose, but that also seems to be not so unpopular, is 7.Ke3. 

White plays this about 28% of the time, which is north of 270,000 games.

White is in serious trouble after we play Qh4! 

Stockfish can defend this, but 99% of the people online aren't Stockfish!

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n3/8/PPPP2PP.text:
The most popular king move is the safest. 7.Kg1 happens in about 30% of games.

The king is safe from checks for now.

Our queen will arrive on h4 and threaten mate on f2!

This is a terrible move: White is putting the pieces back on the home squares to play another game. 

This happens in roughly 26% of games.

Qh4+ is a lethal check. Since the king is on a bad square, g3 doesn't work.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.text:
The Fried Liver Attack. 

White converges on f7. What can we do?

We can go for a counterattack! 

This is a gambit of our f7-pawn, but if White takes, they can get into a world of trouble.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
White goes for the Italian Game.

We'll develop our other knight, because we're not afraid of the Fried Liver.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White attacks our e5-pawn.

Let's defend our center.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the Traxler! 

This is an aggressive gambit against the Fried Liver Attack. 

There are more than 25 million games played in the Fried Liver, so the chances you'll get to play your Traxler are really high!

White starts with 1.e4.

We'll play 1...e5 to lay claim to the center as well.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/2n2n2/3Bp3/4P3/8/PPPP1b.text: White has missed the point of 7...d5. This move blunders the queen.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/2n2n2/3Pp3/2B5/8/PPPP1b.text:
White recaptures and gains a tempo on our knight.

We'll jump into the center with our knight, with the threat of Bg4, trapping White's queen.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/3P1n2/4p3/2Bn4/8/PPPP1b.text:
This continuation is White's best line. It's a key defensive resource, giving White access to f7.

We'll take the pawn with our queen.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/3Pp3/2Bn4/2P5/PP1P1.text:
9.c3 is a critical move, because it opens an escape diagonal for the queen in case of Bg4 and creates a threat on the knight.

Bg4 is still a very strong developing move.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/3Pp3/2Bn4/3P4/PPP2b.text:
d3 is the most played move. It opens the dark-squared bishop and creates an escape on d2 for the white queen.

Bg4 is still a very strong developing move.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/3Pp3/2Bn4/8/PPPP1KP.text:
Maybe White chooses to take the bishop now.

We can land a check. This time we'll put the knight on g4.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/8/3Pp3/2Bn2n1/8/PPPP2PP.text:
Choosing to retreat to e1.

But Qf6, threatening mate, causes problems down the f-file.

r1b1k2N/ppp3pp/5q2/3Pp3/2Bn2n1/8/PPPP2PP.text:
White obviously tries to prevent this...

We'll check on h4.

r1b1k2N/ppp3pp/8/2qPp3/2Bn2n1/8/PPPP2PP/.text: We threaten a deadly discovery, and if the king runs to the f-file, Qf8+ is lethal.

r1b1k2N/ppp3pp/8/3Pp3/2Bn2n1/6P1/PPPP3q/.text: We can capture the recently undefended h2-pawn and continue with a vicious attack against the king.

r1b1k2N/ppppq1pp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.text:
White decides to go up a rook by capturing on h8.

Now that we we have sacrificed the rook, let's focus on attacking the king! 7...d5 opens the position even more. Our light-squared bishop is unleashed with a tempo!

r1b1k3/ppp2Npp/3q1n2/4p3/2Bn4/8/PPPP1bPP.text:
White brings their knight out with a tempo.

We'll deploy the queen to c5, where it is lined up against f2. It also attacks the white bishop.

r1b1k3/ppp2Npp/5n2/2q1p3/2Bn4/3P4/PPP2bP.text:
White defends it.

We develop our last minor piece, attacking the white queen.

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/8/PPP.text:
This is our second study looking at 5.Nxf7.

It looks like we have too many pieces hanging, but we'll sacrifice another to put the White king in danger: Bxf2+!

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.text:
In this chapter we will analyze the positions arising from Kf1, which is the best move, but White's position remains in peril.

It's not the most common move, however, played 41% of the time, which is 662 thousand games.

White is using our bishop as a shield. Let's go ahead and remove our queen from danger.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.text:
White decides to enter the Fried Liver!

...Bc5 is The Traxler counterattack!

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
The Italian game, one of the most popular openings at any level.

We develop our other knight to f6, attacking the e4-pawn.

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/3Pp3/2Bn2b1/3P4/PPPQ1.text:
Qd2 is the only move which prevents the loss of the queen. Now our f2 bishop is really threatened!

Now's the time to save that bishop. Bh4 opens up the f-file for future action.

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/3Pp3/2Bn2bb/2PP4/PP1Q.text:
White decides to attack our knight pushing the c-pawn.

But now we can jump into e4 with the knight, attacking the queen! Of course White can take...

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/3Pp3/Q1Bn2b1/2P5/PP1P.text:
White saves their queen while giving a check.

Let's calmly block the check, while potentially freeing up the f6 square for our queen. The idea of opening up the f-file is very important.

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/8/3Pp3/2BnP1bb/2P5/PP1Q2P.text:
But now the door's wide open! Let's go in.

Qf6+, and we force White into a corner.

r3k2N/ppp3pp/5q2/3Pp3/2BnP1bb/2P5/PP1Q2P.text:
Danger levels! Pause and try to find the move for black!

With Ne2+, we block the queen's vision of the f2 square.

r3k2N/ppp3pp/5q2/3Pp3/4P1bb/2P5/PP1QB1PP.text: White had to take with the queen to avoid immediate checkmate.

r3k2N/pppn2pp/5q2/3Pp3/Q1BP2b1/8/PP1P1bP.text: Qf6 sets up a deadly discovered check. White now can only delay checkmate with ridiculous moves giving away material.

r3k2N/pppn2pp/5q2/3Pp3/Q1Bn2b1/2P3P1/PP1.text: Notice how our bishop prevents the White king from escaping to the queenside.

r3k2N/pppn2pp/7q/3Pp3/Q1Bn2b1/2P5/PP1P1K.text:
Kf2 is forced.

Now Qf4+ comes with devastating effects. The king is forced onto the back rank!

r3k2N/pppn2pp/8/3Pp3/Q1Bn1qb1/2P5/PP1P2P.text:
The king is cornered.

Now Ne2+ and the knight must be taken by the bishop! We'll win the queen next move!

r3k2N/pppn2pp/8/3Pp3/Q1Bn2bq/2P1K3/PP1P2.text:
If the king tries to run, desperatly hoping for an escape via d3-c2...

Qh6+ is a powerful check which forces the king back.

r3k2N/pppn2pp/8/3Pp3/Q1Bn2bq/2P3P1/PP1P1.text:
White tries to block the check with the pawn, hoping to create a shield. Now the light squares around the king are really weak.

We switch back with the queen. Qf6+ basically guarantees the win for Black. Now White is forced to the back rank.

r3k2N/pppn2pp/8/3Pp3/Q4qb1/2P5/PP1PB1PP/.text: The bishop has to take. It's the only legal move.

r3k2N/pppn2pp/8/3Pp3/q5b1/2P5/PP1PB1PP/R.text: White has lost the queen, and will probably have a tough time developing that queenside. By the time they manage to move, you should be able to mate the king or simply gain more material.

r3k2N/pppn2pp/8/3Ppq2/Q1Bn2b1/2P3P1/PP1P.text: Qf5! A slow move that secures the advantage: we're infiltrating on the light squares.

r3k2N/pppnq1pp/8/3Pp3/Q1BP2b1/8/PP1P1bPP.text: A common blunder... We are currently down 9 points of material, but our attack is crushing.

r3k2N/pppnq1pp/8/3Pp3/Q1Bn2b1/2P5/PP1P1K.text:
11.Kxf2 is by far the funniest line in the chapter... just that only we get a laugh! The White king is left exposed on f2.

Now 11...Qh4+ is a very tricky check.

r3k3/ppp2Npp/5n2/2q1p3/2Bn2b1/3P4/PPPQ1b.text: White moves it to safety, attacking our bishop.

r3k3/ppp2Npp/5n2/2q1p3/2Bn2bb/3P4/PPPQ2P.text:
We retreat! White still has a lot of problems to solve. The immediate issues are ...Be2+ and ...b5.

Keep in mind you don't have to memorize the entirety of this continuation, but merely understand the ideas within this system.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White develops the knight, targeting the e5 pawn.

We'll develop our knight as well, defending e5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In this study you'll learn how to crush people with the Traxler in the positions that may arise after we take on f2 and White goes 6.Kf1.

White starts off in the most traditional way, pushing the king's pawn in the center.

We'll mirror White's opening with 1...e5.

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/4p1N1/1P1P4/8/PP3PqP.text:
But we take on g2, attacking the rook! White can easily go wrong here.

Qf3 is the only real defense, and the queens will come off. But we'll still be causing trouble with moves such as ...e4 and Nxb4, giving us active compensation for our piece deficit.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/3p1q2/n1b1p1N1/2B1P3/3P4.text:
We develop the queen while attacking f2.

Next, we can push the knight back with ...h6, or seize the bishop pair by capturing on c4.

r1bnk2r/ppp2ppp/5n2/2P1p1N1/2p1P3/8/PPP2.text: We recapture with the knight and have an equal endgame.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np1n1p/2b1p3/2B1P3/2NP.text:
After they retreat...

We'll create a pin.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np1n1p/2b1p3/2B1P3/2PP.text:
The knight retreats...

And we'll pin it to the queen.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b1p1N1/2B1P3/2N.text:
White develops a knight.

And we kick the other knight back.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2b1p1N1/2B1P3/2P.text:
White plays c3, in preparation of d4.

Let's kick the knight out.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2bNp1N1/2B1P3/3P.text:
White offers a minor piece trade.

But we'll aim to trade off White's good bishop on c4.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/2B1P3/2N.text:
White pushes d3.

We'll push d6 ourselves.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/2B1P3/3P.text:
d3 supports e4 and prepares to develop the bishop on c1.

We'll play d6 and do likewise.

White also castles.

We'll prepare to develop our bishop.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/2Ppp1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.text:
Should White take our bishop...

We'll take theirs.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/2bBp1N1/3PP3/8/PPP.text:
The bishop can also take.

We'll give an intermezzo check.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/2bPp1N1/2BP4/8/PPP.text:
Should White take the pawn, attacking our knight...

We'll get the knight out of danger and remove the attacker of our bishop, too.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3Bp1N1/1b1PP3/2P5/.text:
White blocks it.

We'll take the bishop on d5.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3Pp1N1/1b1P4/2P5/PP3.text:
White recaptures.

But this allows us to activate our queen.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/5n2/2bPp1N1/2Bn4/8/PPP2P.text:
White gets to safety, but...

We can develop with a tempo on the queen.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/2B1P3/2N5.text:
White goes for piece development, but it's questionable whether this is what the position requires. 

This move is only played 1% of the time and doesn't seem natural, because it gives us time to castle, which we'll do straightaway!

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/2B1P3/3P4.text:
White attempts to be solid, supporting their center with d3.

5.d3 is only played 1% of the time.

But we can get our king to safety and then question White's knight on g5.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/2B1P3/8/P.text:
White chooses safety before the attack! 

Around 6% of players don't want to get into the tricky Traxler lines.

That's about 200,000 games.

We'll also castle. We're now guarding f7!

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/2BPP3/8/P.text:
White chooses to break in the center! But we have a move of our own! 

This move is played 1% of the time, but is extremely confrontational, so we need to learn how to play against it!

Let's push with d5, attacking the bishop!

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.text:
White defends e4 and converges on f7!

But we'll ignore the incoming attack and target f2!

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
White develops with an eye on f7.

We'll develop, attacking e4.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np1n1p/2b1p2b/2B1P1P1/2.text:
And g4 is a mistake.

We can sacrifice a piece and maintain the pin.

White cannot stubbornly remove the pin.

We'll simply hit them with the knight sacrifice on g4.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np1n1p/2b1p3/2B1P1b1/2N.text:
White tries to remove the pin.

But we can just maintain it.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np1n1p/2b1p3/2B1P1b1/2P.text:
White attacks us.

We'll maintain the pin.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np3p/2b1p3/2B1P1b1/2NP1.text: But the pin is revived and our knight can even jump to d4 next move to attack the pinned knight.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/2np3p/2b1p3/2B1P1b1/2PP1.text: We can maintain the pin to much success.

r2qk2r/ppp2pp1/5n1p/2bPp3/2B5/5n1P/PPPQ1.text: That's a fork. We win White's queen!

r2qk2r/ppp2pp1/5n1p/2bPp3/2Bn2b1/7N/PPPQ.text:
And once they retreat the knight...

We can take it.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/5n2/2bPp1N1/2Bn2b1/8/PPPQ.text:
White attempts to move out of danger.

But we'll kick the knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White attacks e5.

We'll defend the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
This is the fourth study of the Traxler. Previously, we saw Bxf7+ on move 5. 

But what if White goes for something else on move 5, like castling, d4 trying to open the position up, d3 being timid, or just development with Nc3? 

White opens with the king's pawn.

We mirror White's choice.

2rqr1k1/pp3pb1/4bn1p/P3N1p1/3Pp3/1B6/1P3.text: Now we take control of the c-file. As is apparent in the current position, Black has good major piece activity. Meanwhile White struggles to find a plan, whereas we can continue with piling up the pressure on the isolated pawn.

r1b1k3/ppp1qpb1/2np1n2/3Bp1Br/3PP1pp/2P5.text: White can attempt to trade a piece.

r1b2rk1/ppp1qpb1/2n2npp/4p3/PPB1P3/2P2N2.text:
White continues expanding.

We'll bring our rook to d8.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pb1/2n2npp/4p3/P1B1P3/2P2N2.text:
White proceeds with queenside expansion.

We'll bring our queen out, supporting our pawn, while vacating the d8 square for a rook.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pb1/2np1n1p/4p1p1/2N1P3/1BP.text:
White goes to the nice c4 square with the knight. This move makes a d5 push slightly more difficult for us.

Let's develop, hitting that knight and opposing White's bishop.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pb1/2np1npp/4P3/2B1P3/2P2N2.text:
White can choose to take in the center.

But we can recapture with the pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppp2pb1/2np1n1p/4p1p1/4P3/1BPP1N.text:
White retreats to preserve their bishop against any attacks.

Let's get our king to safety.

r1bqk2r/ppp2pb1/2np1n2/4p1B1/2BPP1pp/2P5.text:
White pins us!

Let's attack the white bishop with ...Rh5!

r1bqk2r/ppp2pb1/2np1npp/4p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/.text:
White castles...

And so will we.

r1bqk3/ppp2pb1/2np1n2/4p1Br/2BPP1pp/2P5/.text:
The queen defends.

We'll bring our queen forward in preparation for getting our king to safety.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2p2/2np1n1p/4p1p1/2B1P3/2PP1.text:
White supports e4 with the knight. 

It's played 12% of the time at this point.

Let's just fianchetto.

White supports e4 before pushing d4.

This logical move is chosen 18% of the time.

Let's continue marching on the kingside!

r1bqkb1r/ppp2p2/2np1n1p/4p3/2B1P1p1/2PP4.text:
White retreats.

What about this logical move, defending e4?

We can take it anyways!

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.text:
What about c3, preparing d4? 

It's only played 4% of the time, and that's because...

We can simply take the unprotected e-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
What if White just castles, contending that perhaps Re1 after we capture on e4 will give them sufficient counterplay? 

This move is played 10% of the time, which is around 7.5 million games.

We are happy to test our their idea! We'll capture the pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/3Bp3/4n3/5N2/PPPP1.text:
Now this is the top computer move, forking both knights, one of which (the knight on c6) is the defender of e5.

Even though it's only played 4% of the time, you might just face it against a prepared opponent.

We can retreat, attacking the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1N3/5N2/PPPP.text: Once White captures, we've got the famous "center fork trick."

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1n3/2P2N2/PP.text:
White can pretend they'll be dynamic and get activity for the pawn.

We've got to be used to this move by now, attacking the bishop and defending our knight on e4.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1n3/5N2/PPPP.text:
White can bring the rook to the e-file, opposite our king. 

Expect to see this move about half the time.

The response to this is to defend the knight and attack the bishop at once!

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2BPn3/2P2N2/PP.text:
White can continue with their original idea of d4!

Let's play the same old move we're used to, attacking the bishop and defending our knight.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
The bishop is taken out in standard Italian fashion.

And we'll develop and attack e4.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2pp1/2pb1n1p/4N3/3P3B/2N5/PP.text: White develops the knight with the idea of jumping to e4 and applying pressure on our pinned knight.

r2qr1k1/ppp2pp1/2pb1n1p/4Nb2/3P3B/2N5/PP.text:
We therefore develop the bishop and cover e4.

We have a comfortable position.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White attacks e5.

We'll develop and defend it.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In this study we'll go over some deviations which aren't particularly good for White, but you might indeed see them in an actual game, especially at lower levels. We're talking about move 4 choices by White which we can exploit. These moves are 4.0-0/c3/Nc3. 

So let's begin with 1.e4 e5!
